title: CAPITAL IDEAS: The lag 7 — Is Micron the new Nvidia?
text:
My rule of thumb, which I borrowed from DataTrek, is that a double is a bubble. If a company’s stock price doubles within a year, there is a good chance the price has advanced much faster than the fundamentals.
Big Tech leadership is shifting. The Magnificent 7 and Broadcom weakened in June, while the broader market held up better than expected and Micron surged.
Investors should respect both the opportunity and the risk. Micron’s growth, margins, and role in AI memory are impressive, but its rapid stock rise has started to look bubble-like.
Bottom line: Micron is not the new Nvidia, but it is a serious AI beneficiary. The stock may still have long-term potential, but position size and diversification matter more after such a huge run.
Two years ago, the darling of Wall Street was Nvidia , the technology company that sells graphics processing units (GPUs) used by artificial intelligence companies.
That was two years ago. As Barron’s recently referenced, Micron is the new Nvidia.
Micron’s stock is up about 855 percent in the last 12 months, while Nvidia traded down over 15 percent from its June 2, 2026, high. In fairness, June 2026 was a harsh month for many technology stocks. Nvidia’s stock was down about five percent in June; however, Micron’s stock shook off the June swoon and was up about 19 percent.
It’s not just Nvidia that got smashed in June. Nearly all of the so-called Magnificent 7 stocks, plus Broadcom, are below their respective 50-day moving averages (Tesla being the exception), a sign that price weakness is becoming a trend. Those eight stocks account for about 34 percent of the S&P 500; each was down roughly three percent to 17 percent in June.
Despite over one-third of the S&P 500’s market capitalization taking it on the chin in June, the index itself was down only about one percent and remained around its 50-day moving average. That is because the next 492 stocks were up an average of two percent.
(To briefly address the concentration, two years ago, that was often cited as a major risk to the stock market. In November 2024, the eight largest companies at the time represented 33.5 percent of the S&P 500—nearly identical to today. I wrote then, “It is OK for the S&P 500 to have a handful of companies representing a large percentage of the index.” I don’t have any reason to feel differently today; the index is up about 25 percent since then.)
As you will recall, the S&P 500 is market-cap weighted, and it was down about one percent in June. In contrast, the equal-weighted S&P 500 index, often represented by the RSP ETF, was up by about 1.9 percent. The correlation between market-cap and the equal-weighted S&P 500 is at a record low.
Based on the performance of the biggest eight stocks, it is no wonder that the S&P 500 stalled out after hitting a high on June 2. Based on the performance of the other 492 stocks, it is no wonder that the index was only down about one percent from its recent high as of the end of June, which is not a lot.
Interestingly, the S&P 500 is up about 9.5 percent year to date, but over the same period, the forward price-to-earnings ratio has contracted nearly 10 percent. That is because earnings of the companies in that index have been incredible, with roughly an 18 percent growth rate for the first half of 2026, and Q2 expected to be above 20 percent.
That trend—rising stock prices and simultaneously improving valuations—is very bullish. I have doubts that the earnings growth rate can continue at that pace, but it is not impossible. I mean, it just happened, so we know it is not impossible.
For earnings to keep improving, we need 1) lower oil prices (which seems to be happening), 2) the AI-related infrastructure buildout to continue (I suspect it will through the next 12 months), and 3) interest rates to stay where they are, or go lower (but the futures market says they will go higher). So, two out of three ain’t bad, and it is probably enough to keep the economy from slipping into a recession and keep the stock market from crashing. But two out of three probably isn’t enough for stocks to rocket higher either.
It seems worth staying invested, even if the S&P pullback hits double digits in the short term. Unfortunately, that short-term pain is the entry fee for the potential of long-term rewards.
Despite the weakness in large technology stocks, Micron has had enough positive performance to push it into the coveted trillion-dollar club. Apple was the first company to reach a $1 trillion market capitalization, and at the time, many people thought it was so outlandish a number that it would signal a market top. Apple hit $1 trillion in 2018; now there are 17 companies in the trillion-dollar club.
Is Micron the new Nvidia?
Two years ago, investors kept asking if it was too late to buy Nvidia . I wrote about this on July 22, 2024. Since then, Nvidia’s stock is up about 55 percent, compared to the S&P 500’s 32 percent. Micron, though, has soared about 937 percent since then.
Micron makes memory and storage chips that help computers, phones, cars, data centers, and AI systems store and quickly access data.
Make no mistake about it, memory stocks are starting to feel bubble-like. Micron has been one of the best-performing stocks in the S&P 500 this year, and after its latest earnings report, the stock jumped nearly 16 percent in a single day. Other memory chip companies, such as SK Hynix and Samsung, have also experienced massive runups. When an entire corner of the market starts moving like a meme stock, investors should slow down and ask whether the story has gotten ahead of the math. My rule of thumb, which I borrowed from DataTrek , is that a double is a bubble. If a company’s stock price doubles within a year, there is a good chance the price has advanced much faster than the fundamentals.
I invested in the Invesco AI and Next Gen Software ETF (NOT an investment recommendation), which had 27 percent of its weighting in memory stocks. Each of the memory stocks in that ETF has way more than doubled. It has been a wild ride up, but I worry that it is on the precipice of a decline. But let’s look at Micron to think about whether a decline is warranted and, if so, if it might be short term or permanent.
In Micron’s case, the math is stunning. For its third fiscal quarter of 2026, Micron reported revenue of $41.46 billion. One year earlier, revenue was $9.30 billion. That is roughly 346 percent revenue growth. GAAP (generally accepted accounting principles) net income was $28.24 billion, compared with $1.89 billion a year ago. Micron’s gross margin was 84.6 percent, up from 37.7 percent a year earlier, and its operating margin was 80.4 percent, up from 23.3 percent. That is actual money hitting the income statement now.
The new Micron is still cyclical, but investors may view the durability of its earnings more favorably because artificial intelligence needs a lot of memory.
A graphics processor (like those designed by Nvidia) powers the AI data center, but memory is just as important. Large AI models need to move huge amounts of data quickly. If data doesn’t reach the processor fast enough, it has to wait, which can be costly.
High-bandwidth memory (HBM) sits close to the AI accelerator and feeds it data at high speed. Storage also matters because training, checkpointing, data retrieval, and inference all require huge amounts of fast, reliable memory and storage infrastructure.
That is why Nvidia’s success is spilling over into Micron. Nvidia remains the king of AI chips. Micron’s latest revenue growth was about 346 percent, compared with Nvidia’s 85 percent. Micron’s GAAP gross margin was 84.6 percent, compared with Nvidia’s 74.9 percent. Micron’s operating margin was 80.4 percent, compared with Nvidia’s roughly 66 percent. Nvidia still earns more dollars. Micron is growing faster right now and, at least in the latest quarter, is showing even fatter margins.
That is why investors are watching closely.
The broader capital-spending backdrop supports the rally. Goldman Sachs estimates annual AI infrastructure capital expenditures could reach $765 billion in 2026 and grow to $1.6 trillion by 2031, with cumulative spending of about $7.6 trillion from 2026 through 2031. That spending includes chips, data centers, power, cooling, networking, and the other plumbing required to run AI at scale. Memory is one of those essential pieces of plumbing.
Unfortunately, the AI boom is not just pushing up prices for the winners. It could also raise costs for everyone else. A shortage of memory might affect the prices of consumer electronics.
Apple said it can no longer absorb the surge in memory and storage costs and announced price increases for some Macs and iPads, citing higher memory costs. When Micron’s profit margins grow, it means higher costs for others. If memory companies earn more, then device makers, server makers, cloud providers, and eventually consumers could end up paying more for electronics.
So, is Micron the new Nvidia?
Memory is now a key asset in the AI economy. But when a stock doubles or more, the risk goes up, even if the business is strong. However, ignoring Micron just because it has risen sharply could be the same mistake many made with Nvidia. Position size and diversification are important.
Nvidia is still the main name in AI, at least until companies like OpenAI and Anthropic go public. Micron and other memory chip makers are becoming key players in this space. I’d say Micron is not the new Nvidia, just a new opportunity (talk to your financial advisor before making any investment). But again, mind your position size and diversification: If you own the S&P 500 index, Micron already accounts for about 1.7 percent of that investment.
Allen Harris is an owner of Berkshire Money Management in Great Barrington and Dalton, managing more than $1 billion of investments.
